To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have cloned the cDNA for the enzyme collagenase, which is responsible for degradation of connective tissue, from rheumatoid synoviocyte mRNA.
a single collagenase mRNA transcript is selected by our cDNA clone from primary cultures of human synovium and that this cDNA identifies a single collagenase genomic DNA sequence.

we have isolated the human collagenase cDNA clone and have shown that this cDNA clone is identical to the human skin collagenase cDNA and that the human skin and synovaial cell collagenases are derived from a single gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation, characterization, and expression of the human collagenase gene and its products, the collagenase protein and messenger RNA (mRNAs).
the identification of the human collagenase gene and the isolation of a full-length complementary DNA (cDNa) clone.
the identification of the genes encoding the collagenases, a family of enzymes that play a major role in the degradation of the extracellular matrix.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human synovial cells and skin fibroblasts produce a similar type of collagenase, which is a single gene product and is not differentially expressed in either cell type.
the collagenase gene is identical in both human skin fibroblasts and rheumatoid synoviocytes and that a single gene is present in the human genome.
the human collagenase gene was cloned and sequenced and that the cDNA hybridized with a single mRNA transcript from rheumatoid synoial fibroblast cell cultures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we cloned the human collagenase cDNA from synovial cell mRNA, and that we used the cDNA probe to identify a single gene from human genomic DNA.
we have identified the gene for human collagenase and that the human collagenase gene is expressed in rheumatoid synoial cells.
the human collagenase cDNA clone is identical to that for human skin fibroblasts and that a single gene for human collagenase has been identified in human DNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the collagenases of skin and synovium are identical, and that the ubiquity of these enzymes and their substrates, the fibrillar collagens, implies that common mechanisms for collagenolysis may be operative in the normal and diseased state.

a single gene codes for human skin and syn ovial cell collagenase, that the gene is present in a single copy in the human genome, and that the gene is transcribed to produce mRNA in human skin and synovi al cells.
we identified the gene encoding the human collagenase enzyme.
